impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims against the government in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether the Federal Circuit's prior holding in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is not subject to American Pipe class action tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision. The court affirmed dismissal of breach of contract and takings claims by bank holding company shareholders who lost significant assets during the 2008 financial crisis when the government placed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship.
impacts.negativeImplications: Eliminates American Pipe tolling for claims against the federal government under § 2501, meaning businesses and investors in class actions against the government cannot rely on the filing of a class action to toll the statute of limitations for individual claims. This increases the risk that individual claims will be time-barred if a class action fails.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when calculating copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes a legally permissible application of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine in assessing damages against the government for software copyright infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's use of a hypothetical negotiation rather than existing license terms to calculate copyright infringement damages for the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software. However, the court vacated the damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies that copyright holders are not limited to existing license rates when proving infringement damages, potentially enabling higher recovery through hypothetical negotiation frameworks. Software companies benefit from the court's recognition that unauthorized government copying constitutes infringement.
impacts.negativeImplications: The court's rejection of non-compensatory damages and limitation of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine may constrain the damages theories available to software companies in government infringement cases, potentially reducing recovery amounts.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether broad method claims reciting the use of a genus of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache satisfy the enablement requirement, and whether the enablement standards applied to composition claims in Amgen v. Sanofi apply equally to method claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headaches using anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims, undermines medical innovation by sustaining overly broad claims, and conflicts with Supreme Court enablement precedent in Amgen v. Sanofi.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method claims in the pharmaceutical and biotech space benefit from the court's apparent willingness to apply less stringent enablement analysis to method claims than to composition claims, potentially preserving broader patent protection for therapeutic methods.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and generic drug manufacturers face potentially broader patent barriers, as broad method claims covering large genera of compounds may be more difficult to design around or invalidate on enablement grounds. The dissent's concerns suggest continued uncertainty and potential future reversal.

impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit's pre-AIA written description analysis from Dynamic Drinkware applies to prior art determinations under AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(d)(2), specifically whether a reference patent must have at least one claim supported by a provisional application's written description to receive the provisional's filing date as prior art.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's decision finding Dental Monitoring's patent claims obvious and remanded for further consideration, addressing the critical question of when a reference patent can claim the benefit of a provisional application's filing date for prior art purposes under the AIA. The Board had relied on its Penumbra precedent to reject the Dynamic Drinkware written description requirement for AIA cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders may benefit from a stricter standard for establishing prior art effective dates, potentially narrowing the universe of prior art references that can be used to challenge patents in IPR proceedings. This could make it harder to invalidate patents based on provisional application filing dates.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges to competitor patents face greater uncertainty about what qualifies as prior art under the AIA, potentially increasing costs and complexity of patent validity challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive licensee that shifted its business operations to patent enforcement had 'ceased its business operations' triggering automatic termination of its license agreement, and whether the license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations under its license agreement with Texas A&M University. The court further held that the exclusive license conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M as a co-plaintiff.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees benefit from the court's recognition that patent enforcement activities constitute ongoing business operations and that broad exclusive licenses can convey sufficient rights to sue independently, reducing procedural barriers to enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face increased enforcement exposure from exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities, as the ruling makes it harder to challenge standing based on license termination or failure to join the patent owner.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations used in digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and the proper framework for analyzing eligibility of claims that improve technological systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims related to non-uniform constellation designs used in TV broadcasting while affirming eligibility for other claims, affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings, and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved a jury verdict against LG for willfully infringing communication technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: The affirmance of eligibility for certain claims and the damages award provides guidance on when technology-improvement claims survive § 101 challenges, benefiting patent holders in the communications technology space.
impacts.negativeImplications: The partial vacatur on eligibility grounds introduces continued uncertainty for patent holders with claims at the boundary of abstract ideas and technological improvements, particularly in the communications standards space where billions in licensing revenue are at stake.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement phrase 'survives the EPR' (ex parte reexamination), or whether such a contract interpretation dispute must be heard by the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit transferred a case to the Fifth Circuit, holding it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent settlement payment after asserted patent claims survived reexamination without amendment. The court ruled that the dispute was fundamentally about contract interpretation under Texas law, not patent law, even though it arose from a patent litigation settlement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity on jurisdictional boundaries for patent settlement agreement disputes, potentially allowing parties to litigate contract claims in more convenient regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates complexity for parties drafting patent settlement agreements with contingent payment terms, as disputes may end up in regional circuits less experienced with patent-related concepts like reexamination outcomes. Increases forum uncertainty for settlement enforcement disputes.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint without granting leave to amend and whether attorney fee awards under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 were appropriate where the plaintiff's counsel implicitly agreed not to amend in exchange for a filing extension.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a patent infringement case with prejudice, its denial of leave to amend, and its award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285. The court found the case exceptional where the plaintiff implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint in exchange for an extension, then attempted to amend anyway, and where the proposed amended complaint was futile.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defendants' ability to recover fees in exceptional patent cases and deters frivolous patent infringement litigation. Provides guidance that implicit agreements not to amend complaints are enforceable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face heightened risk of fee awards and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims that prove meritless, especially where related patent claims have been rejected or invalidated on § 101 grounds.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus using a transformer with a non-magnetic core to match impedance for wireless signal transmission are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even where the district court erroneously found indefiniteness.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds, holding that Samsung demonstrated the asserted claims of the '385 patent were not enabled. The court reached the enablement issue as an alternative ground for affirmance even though the district court had not addressed it.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not reached below, potentially reducing the need for costly retrials. Strengthens enablement as a defense against broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that appellate courts will affirm invalidity on grounds not litigated at trial, limiting their ability to present evidence and arguments on alternative invalidity theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such a deadline.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day participation deadline for antidumping duty sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The statute is silent on when interested parties must respond to a notice of initiation, and the regulatory deadline was the product of reasoned decisionmaking within the bounds of the agency's power.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers benefit from clear procedural rules for participating in sunset reviews that protect against premature revocation of antidumping duty orders. The ruling upholds Commerce's authority to establish reasonable deadlines for trade remedy proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign exporters and importers face a relatively short 15-day window to indicate participation in sunset reviews, with failure to meet the deadline potentially resulting in continuation of antidumping duties without full adversarial proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess en banc framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences between claimed and accused designs rather than overall similarity, and whether 'claim construction' of design patents improperly resolves factual functionality questions that should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent infringement case, with significant disagreement among the judges. The concurrence defended the Egyptian Goddess framework as consistent with Supreme Court precedent, while the dissent (joined by four judges) argued the framework improperly shifts the infringement analysis toward differences and allows courts to resolve factual functionality questions at summary judgment rather than sending them to juries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Design patent defendants benefit from the continued application of the Egyptian Goddess framework, which allows courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment when claimed and accused designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face a significant split among Federal Circuit judges on the proper infringement standard, creating uncertainty. Four judges dissented, suggesting the current framework may be revisited and potentially changed, destabilizing design patent enforcement strategies.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court must provide sufficient detail in denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 to permit meaningful appellate review, particularly where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after the PTO rejected related patent claims under § 101 and a district court invalidated a related patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded a district court's denial of sanctions and fees motions, holding that the court's order provided insufficient detail for meaningful review. The case involved a patent holder that pursued infringement claims on a patent related to electronic sweepstakes systems despite multiple PTO § 101 rejections of related applications and a sister court's invalidation of a related patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's insistence on detailed analysis of exceptional-case determinations, which may increase the likelihood of fee awards in cases where patent holders pursue claims despite strong indicators of invalidity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face heightened scrutiny when pursuing infringement claims on patents related to applications or patents that have been rejected or invalidated on eligibility grounds, with potential fee-shifting consequences.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent case on both improper venue and patent eligibility grounds in the same order, or whether it must transfer or dismiss for improper venue without reaching the merits.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of a patent infringement case on both improper venue and § 101 patent eligibility grounds, rejecting AML's argument that the court should not have reached the eligibility issue after finding venue improper. The case involved e-commerce method patents challenged as abstract ideas.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals simultaneously with venue-based dismissals, preventing patent holders from simply refiling in a new venue after a § 101 determination.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face the risk that a venue challenge will be accompanied by a merits-based invalidity determination that has preclusive effect in subsequent litigation, even if the case could have been refiled elsewhere.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent claiming drug-releasing biodegradable polymer fiber compositions used in coronary stent systems was anticipated by prior art and whether the accused products infringed the asserted claims.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding that Boston Scientific infringed the University of Texas's drug-eluting stent patent, holding that BSC was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court overturned the jury's findings on both liability theories, eliminating a damages award in a significant medical device patent case.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the court's willingness to grant JMOL overturning jury verdicts on both anticipation and non-infringement, providing greater certainty against patent claims in the coronary stent space.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and licensors face risk that jury verdicts in their favor may be reversed on appeal, undermining the value of patent portfolios in the medical device field and reducing leverage in licensing negotiations.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's original methodology for determining whether government debt-to-equity conversions conferred countervailable benefits was proper, and whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's remand determination finding no countervailable benefit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and ordered reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean steel company conferred countervailable benefits, rejecting the under-protest remand determinations. The decision restores countervailing duties on imported steel products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from reinstatement of countervailing duties that offset foreign government subsidies, leveling the competitive playing field for imports. Strengthens Commerce's authority to apply its preferred methodologies for assessing equity infusion benefits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face reinstated countervailing duties and reduced flexibility to challenge Commerce's benefit calculations through court-ordered remands.
